title: Reading a wave formula, and the acoustics vocabulary
summary: Look at A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) and say what each symbol does; picture it as a point going around a circle; use frequency/period/amplitude/dB/spectrum correctly; predict how a plot changes when one dial changes.
sourceNote: basic_acoustics.pdf (Day 2), sinusoids_review.pdf and basic_sinusoids.pdf (Day 3), Lab 1, Lab 3 Q1–Q4.

sections.heading: Why the whole course is one formula

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Where this is going** Speech is a pressure wave. Koo's course says: ==any wave, no matter how messy, can be written as a sum of simple waves called sinusoids== (that's Fourier analysis, Days 5–7). So if you can read one sinusoid — A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) — you can read the building block of everything after. Every lab so far has been a question about one of the four letters in that formula. This chapter makes them yours.
You told me you know the unit circle and radians. Good — that's the only prerequisite. The formula is the unit circle with a clock attached.

blocks.body: A **sound wave** is a pattern of pressure fluctuation caused by the movement of a source (vocal folds) and propagated through a medium (air). A **waveform** is a graph of that pressure over time: x-axis time, y-axis pressure.

how long one cycle takes, in seconds. **Frequency F**: how many cycles per second, in **Hertz (Hz)**. They're reciprocals: **F = 1/T**, **T = 1/F**. A 10 Hz wave has period 0.1 s = 100 ms. (You got this one right: T = 0.01 s → F = 100 Hz.)

how far the wave deviates from rest. **Peak amplitude** is the maximum; **RMS amplitude** (root mean square) is the square root of the average squared value — for a sinusoid with peak 1, RMS = 0.707. RMS is what 'how loud on average' means.
= repeats at regular intervals (a vowel, a tuning fork). **Aperiodic** = no repetition (noise, 's', 'sh').

blocks.md: Loudness doesn't track pressure linearly — doubling the pressure doesn't sound twice as loud — so we compare sounds on a log scale. Here is where the formula comes from: a **bel** is log₁₀ of the ratio of two *intensities*, and intensity goes with amplitude *squared*, so with amplitudes x and r: bels = log₁₀(x²/r²) = 2·log₁₀(x/r). A bel turns out to be too big a unit to be handy, so we report tenths of one: **dB = 10·log₁₀(x²/r²) = 20·log₁₀(x/r)**. Reading the symbols: x is the amplitude you're measuring, r is the reference you're comparing it against, and the log turns ratios into sums — every ×10 in amplitude is +20 dB, stackable. !!Using 10·log₁₀ on amplitudes is the classic slip!! — the 20 is 10 (deci) × 2 (the square), and the bare 10·log₁₀ belongs to intensity/power only.
blocks.slide: Decibels: why the formula has a 20 in it

blocks.title: Code
blocks.body:
amplitude ratio x/r     dB = 20·log10(x/r)
   1 (same)                 0 dB
   2                       +6 dB     ← double the amplitude
  10                      +20 dB
 100                      +40 dB
   0.5                     −6 dB
reference r:  dB SPL → r = 20 μPa (quietest audible 1 kHz tone)
              dB SL  → r = the hearing threshold at THAT frequency

blocks.md: The **equal-loudness curve** slide says: at 50 Hz you need about 40 dB SPL to *just hear* a tone — 100 times the pressure you'd need at 1000 Hz. ##Ears are most sensitive around 1–4 kHz, exactly where speech lives##.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** dB is the unit on every fader, microphone spec, and volume slider you'll ever touch — '6 dB = double the amplitude' is arithmetic audio engineers do without a calculator. The equal-loudness curve is quietly one of the most profitable graphs ever drawn: ==MP3 and AAC compress audio by throwing away the frequency components the curve says you can't hear== — quiet sounds masked by loud neighbors, and anything where the ear is insensitive. And streaming services normalize every track to a target loudness (LUFS, an RMS-style measure) so playlists don't lurch between whisper and blast; that's RMS amplitude doing real work.

blocks.prompt: Lab-style: two vowels, (a) has peak 0.3 and (b) has peak 0.6. Which is louder, and by how many dB?

sections.heading: A sinusoid is a point going around a circle

blocks.md: Draw a circle of radius 1. Put a point on it at angle θ from the positive x-axis. Its coordinates are (cos θ, sin θ). Now let the point *rotate* counterclockwise: θ grows, and if you plot the x-coordinate against θ you get a **cosine wave**; plot the y-coordinate and you get a **sine wave**. ==A sinusoid is the shadow of a rotating point== — that's the whole object. Everything else in the formula is dials.

blocks.slide: The shadow of a rotating point

blocks.body: cosine is sine shifted a quarter cycle earlier. Same shape, different starting point. Koo uses cosine as the standard.

cos(−θ) = cos θ. Rotating clockwise gives the same x-coordinate. **sin is odd**: sin(−θ) = −sin θ. (You said you know these — they're the reason 2cos(2π·(−100)·t − π/3) equals 2cos(2π·100·t + π/3): negate the whole inside and cosine doesn't care.)

blocks.md:
- Both repeat every **2π radians** (360°): cos(θ + 2πk) = cos θ for any integer k. So adding or subtracting 2π inside the parentheses changes nothing — that's Lab 3 Q3.
- Radians: θ = arc length / radius. Full circle = 2π. 90° = π/2, 60° = π/3, 45° = π/4, 30° = π/6.
blocks.slide: Facts about sin and cos you'll use in every lab

blocks.md: The circle picture uses an angle θ; sound happens in time. So let the point rotate at a steady speed: **F rotations per second**. Each rotation is 2π radians, so after t seconds the angle is θ = 2πF·t — ==that substitution is the entire derivation==. Replace θ and cos θ becomes **cos(2πFt)**: a wave that completes F cycles every second, i.e. frequency F Hz. Reading the symbols: t is the clock in seconds, F converts seconds to cycles, and 2π converts cycles to radians — the unit the cosine actually eats. (2πF together is called the angular frequency ω, in radians per second; you'll see ω in readings, F in Koo's notebooks.)

blocks.title: Changing the dials
blocks.body:
Start from x(t) = 2cos(2π·100·t + π/3).

1. Q2: peak amplitude 3× and frequency 2× → change A to 6 and F to 200, leave ϕ: **6cos(2π·200·t + π/3)**. The phase is a starting angle; scaling amplitude or speed doesn't move the start.
2. Q3: which formulas are the *same* wave? Any that differ only by ±2π inside (2cos(… − 5π/3) since π/3 − 2π = −5π/3; 2cos(… + 13π/3) since π/3 + 4π = 13π/3), by negating the whole inside (cos is even: 2cos(2π·(−100)·t − π/3)), or by switching to sine with +π/2 (2sin(2π·100·t + π/3 + π/2) = 2sin(… + 5π/6); and since sin is odd, −2sin(2π·(−100)·t − 5π/6) is the same; and 2sin(… − 7π/6) since 5π/6 − 2π = −7π/6). All six listed options were equivalent — the trick was that none was a distractor.
3. Q4: sampling at Fₛ, taking sample n at time t = n/Fₛ → replace t: **x[n] = 2cos(2π·100·n/Fₛ + π/3)**. Only t changes; A, F, ϕ stay.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) is the signal generator inside every synthesizer oscillator, hearing-test tone, and Web Audio `OscillatorNode` — when a tuner app says A = 440 Hz, that's the F dial by name. Every DAW and every Zoom call is shipping sums of these around at some sample rate. ##Phase, the dial everyone forgets, pays rent too##: noise-cancelling headphones emit the same wave with ϕ shifted by π so the pressures cancel, and two microphones mixed with mismatched phase hollow a recording out. When Days 5–7 take speech apart into sinusoids, 'amplitude, frequency, phase — per component' is the complete answer format, and it's these three dials.

blocks.prompt: Write a 440 Hz wave with amplitude 0.5 that starts at its trough.
blocks.answer: Trough means cos(ϕ) = −1, so ϕ = π: x(t) = 0.5·cos(2π·440·t + π). (Equivalently −0.5·cos(2π·440·t).)

blocks.prompt: How does the plot of 3cos(2π·5·t) change if you (a) change 3 to 10, (b) change 5 to 10, (c) add + π inside?
blocks.answer: (a) Same shape, taller: swings ±10 instead of ±3. (b) Twice as many cycles per second — the wave is squeezed horizontally, period drops from 0.2 s to 0.1 s. (c) Flipped: it starts at its trough instead of its peak (cos(θ + π) = −cos θ).

blocks.body: x(t) = A·cos(2πFt + ϕ): a point of radius A rotating F times per second starting at angle ϕ, seen from the side. A = peak amplitude, F = frequency in Hz, ϕ = initial phase in radians.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why we need spectra** A single sinusoid is a **simple** periodic wave. A vowel is a **complex** periodic wave — it repeats, but the shape inside each cycle is jagged. Day 2's key claim: ==a complex wave is a sum of simple waves== (sinusoids) at different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. A **spectrum** is the recipe: which sinusoids, how much of each.

rows: how much of each frequency is present — a snapshot
the starting angle of each component
darkness/color = amplitude: how the spectrum changes over time
blocks.slide: Three plots you must be able to tell apart

blocks.md: Speech has two parts. The **source** (vocal-fold vibration) produces a buzz with a fundamental frequency F₀ and harmonics at 2F₀, 3F₀, … — these are the **spectral details**, the fine comb of lines in a spectrum. The **filter** (the shape of the mouth and throat) boosts some frequencies and damps others — that's the **spectral envelope**, the smooth outline over the comb; its peaks are the **formants** that make /i/ sound different from /a/. Lab 1 Q6 asked which column of plots showed the filter: the smooth envelopes, not the jagged combs.

blocks.caption: A vowel's magnitude spectrum: the thin lines are harmonics (source detail), the smooth curve is the envelope (filter). The humps in the envelope are formants F1, F2, F3.

blocks.prompt: Lab 1 Q5: on average, which vowel has the higher frequency — (a) or (b)? How do you read that off a waveform?
blocks.answer: Count cycles in the same span of time: the waveform with more (tighter) wiggles per second has the higher fundamental frequency. Amplitude (Q4) is the height of the swings. Read the plot, don't guess from the vowel.

blocks.prompt: You see a plot with time on x, frequency on y, and dark bands. What is it, and what are the bands?
blocks.answer: A spectrogram. Dark horizontal bands are formants (the filter's resonances) tracking over time; fine horizontal lines, if visible, are harmonics of the source.

exercises.title: Read the formula out loud
exercises.prompt: x(t) = 0.5·cos(400πt − π/2). Give the amplitude, the frequency in Hz, the period in ms, and the phase. Then say in one sentence what the plot looks like compared with cos(400πt).
hints: Match it to the template A·cos(2πFt + ϕ) piece by piece. The number in front is A. The thing multiplying t must be written as 2π·F — rewrite 400π that way.
The usual slip is reading 400 as the frequency. 400π = 2π·200, so F = 200 Hz, not 400. And the phase is −π/2, sign included.
Period is 1/F. Phase −π/2 means the cosine is shifted a quarter turn *later* — which is exactly a sine.
solution: Compared with cos(400πt): half the height, same speed, shifted right by a quarter period (1.25 ms). cos(θ − π/2) = sin(θ), so it's 0.5·sin(400πt).
exercises.why: Every audio, radio, and vibration signal you'll ever meet is described with this one formula, and 'what does this plot look like' from the numbers — without running the code — is the skill Koo's labs test and the skill that lets you sanity-check a spectrogram at a glance.

exercises.title: Decibels without a calculator
exercises.prompt: Sound A has amplitude 10 times sound B. Sound C has amplitude 1000 times B. How many dB is A above B, and C above B? Then: if a signal is +6 dB relative to another, roughly what is the amplitude ratio?
hints: dB = 20·log₁₀(x/r). For A/B the ratio is 10; what's log₁₀ of 10? Multiply by 20.
The common error is using 10·log instead of 20·log. Koo's convention for amplitude is 20·log₁₀. (10·log is for power.)
For +6 dB, solve 20·log₁₀(ratio) = 6 → log₁₀(ratio) = 0.3 → ratio = 10^0.3. You know 10^0.3 ≈ 2 because 2³ = 8 ≈ 10 → log₁₀ 2 ≈ 0.3.
solution: +6 dB ↔ amplitude ratio 10^0.3 ≈ 2. (So 'twice as loud in amplitude' is +6 dB; ten times is +20 dB.)
exercises.why: dB is how every mixing board, microphone spec, and hearing-loss chart is labelled. '6 dB = double' and '20 dB = ten times' are the two numbers audio engineers carry in their heads.
